There is every indication that the U.S. economy will continue to meet growing demands placed upon it. Forecasts by Data Resources, Inc. are that real Gross National Product in 1990 will be from 60 to 63 percent greater than in 1976, depending upon which assumptions enter into their forecasts. The U.S. Department of Commerce in its U.S. Industrial Outlook, 1976 includes projections to 1885 which reflect expectations that all major manufacturing and nonmanufacturing sectors will share in GNP growth. This suggests continued and substantial geographical peripheral expansion outside of cities.
To summarize up to this point, it is apparent that: (1) decentralization and sprawl of residences/commerce/industry/institutions has been a strong universal trend, particularly since the end of World War II, (2) populations/commerce/institutions/industry move together, (3) powerful economic, social, and political interactions, interfaces, and interdependencies occur within and between cities and peripheral developments, (4) cities and surrounding areas have not decentralized and expanded geographically in such a uniform manner that a population-mileage formula defines C/Z's-T/A's with the same degree of accuracy for all municipalities in the same population group, (5) continued decentralization and geographical expansion around cities is projected for the foreseeable future, but there are questions as to how the expansion may be distributed among various size cities, and (6) the same forces that caused previous geographical expansion have been reinforced by new ones which seem to outweigh new counteracting forces; they are expected to continue to be the operative forces which will resolve the question of, "In which direction do we grow - up, down, or out?" in favor of continued outward expansion.
